FIGURE 10 Funnel plot showing OR of ATE in the BVZ group versus chemo‐only group with asymmetrical distribution. ATE, arterial thromboembolism; BVZ, bevacizumab. FIGURE 11 Funnel plot showing OR of VTE in the BVZ group versus chemo‐only group with asymmetrical distribution. BVZ, bevacizumab. 4 DISCUSSION BVZ has been used to treat more than 1.56 million patients with mCRC worldwide. 19 Previous RCTs have shown that BVZ, in combination with a standard cytotoxic regime, is safe to administer and without any significant risk of added toxicities. Cardiovascular causes are the number one cause of mortality across the globe, and we need to prevent severe HTN and ATE‐associated mortality with BVZ. Our meta‐analysis is an up‐to‐date study of cardiovascular side effects of BVZ with the largest cohort of patients in the treatment and control groups, increasing the power of the analysis. We analyzed patients across multiple subgroups, taking into account potential confounding factors, to obtain a more refined odds ratio for the given subgroup of patients. We demonstrated that 12.3% of patients develop HTN, 8.2% develop thromboembolism, and 2% develop ATE with BVZ when added to the standard chemotherapy regimen for mCRC. The critical findings in our systematic review and meta‐analysis are as follows. First, BVZ was associated with about four times higher risk of developing HTN than the chemotherapy‐only group. The FOLFOX subgroup analysis, based on the regime used, demonstrated about five times higher odds of developing HTN (Grade 3 or more) in the BVZ + FOLFOX group compared with the FOLFOX‐only group. Our findings are supported by a previous meta‐analysis that reported increased odds of HTN up to five times with BVZ used for CRC and other indications. 20 , 21 , 22 The proposed mechanism for BVZ‐induced HTN, a well‐known side‐effect of the drug, is increased vascular resistance due to the inhibition of vasodilation mediated by vascular endothelial growth factor. However, it has yet to be established as the sole factor for this effect. 9 Our study gives the precise odds of developing grade 3–4 HTN with BVZ, which is essential because, in the literature, a few cases of hypertensive crisis with encephalopathy and subarachnoid hemorrhage have been reported. 24 , 25 , 26 The current AHA guidelines recommend initiation or up‐titration of treatment for secondary HTN due to angiogenesis inhibition by BVZ. 23 An earlier study has shown that temporary discontinuation of BVZ can bring the blood pressure level to pretreatment levels, 28 and such a temporary hold is recommended in cases of refractory HTN on the maximum tolerated antihypertensive regime and hypertensive emergency. 27 Prevention and management of BVZ‐specific HTN is an important aspect of best supportive care during the active treatment phase for mCRC. Second, the odds of thromboembolism in patients managed with BVZ were over 30% higher than in the control group. Our meta‐analysis demonstrates a significant arterial thromboembolic risk of BVZ when added to the advanced CRC treatment standard regime. We found that the odds of getting ATE with BVZ were over two times higher than the chemotherapy‐only control groups. These results affirm the manufacturer's ATE claims and are an area of further research. 27 Previously, studies have tried to evaluate the prophylactic role of aspirin in preventing ATE in patients receiving BVZ but could not conclude. 28 Establishing guidelines to anti‐coagulate patients getting BVZ should be studied. Preventing ATE is crucial in improving the morbidity and mortality associated with BVZ treatment. Our study had several limitations: Firstly, RCTs keep strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Only patients with appropriate major organ functions are included in these trials; therefore, actual patients may not be represented by the results of this meta‐analysis, and our results may not be applicable to the general population in daily practice. Second, although all the studies included RCT, there was a significant difference in the timing and the primary endpoint. The follow‐up time is different from study to study, and there might be unreported events of HTN and thromboembolism after the study was concluded. Third, the studies included in our analysis were heterogeneous regarding patient characteristics across the studies. Fourth, potential differences among the trials may exist as HTN events are collected for each individual trial, such as various international institutions and administration schedules of BVZ increasing the clinical heterogeneity and difficulty in interpreting the analysis results. Finally, the treatment designs varied, and the individual patient data were not focused on in the study. Compared with individual patient data analyses, meta‐analyses based on published data tend to overestimate the treatment effects. 29 Future prospective studies reporting individual subgroup AE data with recurrent, advanced, or mCRC in adjuvant and metastatic settings will help focus on specific subgroups and formulate customized treatment guidelines. There is a significant risk of publication bias based on the funnel plot obtained regarding the review process. Secondly, the incidence of BVZ‐associated HTN, because of the definition of the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), may have been underestimated. Per the CTCAE, blood pressure greater than 150/100 mmHg or diastolic pressure increased by more than 20 mmHg is considered hypertensive. In some studies, these strict criteria would have reduced the number of hypertensive patients noted compared with the clinical criteria for the diagnosis of HTN (140/90 mmHg). CRC is a leading cause of cancer‐related death in the United States. Most patients with mCRC are likely to receive BVZ with adjuvant chemotherapy. Our findings are significant as they provide vital information in assessing the risk–benefit ratio of adding BVZ to the standard chemotherapy in patients with mCRC, especially in patients with vascular comorbidities. Cardiovascular AEs are crucial in determining all‐cause mortality in patients with mCRC. The magnitude of severe HTN, thromboembolic events, and cardiovascular morbidity demonstrated from our meta‐analysis informs oncology clinicians to regularly inform patients and monitor patients with CRC receiving chemotherapy with BVZ. Prevention and management of BVZ‐specific HTN and the ATE episodes in the first place can be essential in mitigating the morbidity and mortality associated with BVZ treatment and is an area of future research in this patient population. Establishing evidence‐based guidelines for blood pressure management and anti‐thrombotic medications will be important for both clinicians and researchers in the future. documents.title: Statins for the primary prevention of venous thromboembolism.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) involves the formation of a blood clot in a vein, and includes deep venous thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE). The annual incidence for VTE varies from 0.75 to 2.69 per 1000 individuals, with about 40 million people worldwide impacted by VTE. Statins, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl (HMG)-coenzyme A (CoA) reductase inhibitors, inhibit cholesterol biosynthesis and display several vascular-protective effects, including antithrombotic properties. However, the potential role of statins in the primary prevention of VTE is still not clear.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the benefits and risks of statins in preventing venous thromboembolism (VTE) in individuals with no prior history of VTE.
SEARCH METHODS: We used standard Cochrane search methods. The search was last updated on 13 March 2023.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing statins with any control intervention (including placebo and usual care) in healthy individuals or participants with conditions other than VTE. There were no restrictions on the dose, duration, route, or timing of statins.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We used standard Cochrane methods. Our primary outcomes were VTE, DVT, and PE. Our secondary outcomes were serious adverse events, adverse events, and mortality. We used the trial sequential analysis (TSA) method to judge whether the evidence was sufficient, and we used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome.
MAIN RESULTS: We included 27 RCTs involving 122,601 adults (aged 18 years and above) who were healthy, had various medical conditions (e.g. hypercholesterolemia), or were at risk for cardiovascular disease. Both males and females were included in all studies. Two studies focused solely on participants over 60 years of age. We deemed four studies to have a low risk of bias overall, while 19 were at high risk of bias, and four were unclear. The 27 studies compared use of statins versus placebo or usual care in individuals who had never experienced VTE. The statins used in the studies were atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, pravastatin, lovastatin, fluvastatin, and simvastatin. Twenty-three studies followed up participants for over a year, with six of those extending follow-ups for over five years. Twenty-five studies were based in hospitals, and 24 studies were funded by industry. Only one study used VTE as a primary endpoint. The median incidence of VTE in the statins group was 0.72% (ranging from 0% to 10.53%), and in the control group it was 0.89% (ranging from 0% to 6.83%). Our pooled analysis of the 27 studies showed that, relative to control groups, statins may slightly reduce the overall incidence of VTE (odds ratio (OR) 0.86, 95% confidence intervals (CI) 0.76 to 0.98; 27 studies, 122,601 participants; low-certainty evidence). Of the statins we evaluated, only rosuvastatin seemed to be associated with a reduced incidence of VTE, albeit the reduction in incidence was very small. The evidence did not clearly indicate a difference between groups in the incidence of DVT (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.18; six studies, 40,305 participants; low-certainty evidence), PE (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.52; five studies, 28,427 participants; low-certainty evidence), or myopathy (OR 1.10, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.45; 10 studies, 75,551 participants; low-certainty evidence). Nonetheless, statin use might slightly decrease the incidence of any serious adverse event (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.99; 13 studies, 67,020 participants; low-certainty evidence) and any death (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.95; 24 studies, 116,761 participants; low-certainty evidence), compared to control.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Using statins for the primary prevention of VTE may slightly reduce the incidence of VTE and all-cause mortality. However, this effect is likely too weak to be considered significant. Statin use may not decrease the occurrence of DVT and PE. The current evidence is insufficient to draw strong conclusions because of the risk of bias in the studies, imprecision in the effect estimates, and potential publication bias. More evidence from well conducted and fully reported RCTs is needed to assess the preventive effects of different types of statins, as well as the effects of different dosages and treatment durations in various populations.

documents.title: Sex as a prognostic factor for mortality in adults with acute symptomatic pulmonary embolism.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is relatively common worldwide. It is a serious condition that can be life-threatening. Studies on the relationship between adverse outcomes of this condition and whether a patient is male or female have yielded inconsistent results. Determining whether there is an association between sex and short-term mortality in patients with acute PE is important as this information may help guide different approaches to PE monitoring and treatment.
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether sex (i.e. being a male or a female patient) is an independent prognostic factor for predicting mortality in adults with acute symptomatic pulmonary embolism.
SEARCH METHODS: The Cochrane Vascular Information Specialist searched the Cochrane Vascular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL databases, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and ClinicalTrials.gov trials register up to 17 February 2023. We scanned conference abstracts and reference lists of included studies and systematic reviews. We also contacted experts to identify additional studies. There were no restrictions with respect to language or date of publication.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included phase 2-confirmatory prognostic studies, that is, any longitudinal study (prospective or retrospective) evaluating the independent association between sex (male or female) and mortality in adults with acute PE.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We followed the Checklist for Critical Appraisal and Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews of prognostic factor studies (CHARMS-PF) and the Cochrane Prognosis Methods Group template for prognosis reviews. Two review authors independently screened the studies, extracted data, assessed the risk of bias according to the Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool, and assessed the certainty of the evidence (GRADE). Meta-analyses were performed by pooling adjusted estimates. When meta-analysis was not possible, we reported the main results narratively.
MAIN RESULTS: We included seven studies (726,293 participants), all of which were retrospective cohort studies with participants recruited and managed in hospitals between 2000 and 2018. Studies took place in the USA, Spain, and Japan. Most studies were multicentre. None were conducted in low- or middle-income countries. The participants' mean age ranged from 62 to 69 years, and the proportion of females was higher in six of the seven studies, ranging from 46% to 60%. Sex and gender terms were used inconsistently. Participants received different PE treatments: reperfusion, inferior vena cava filter, anticoagulation, and haemodynamic/respiratory support. The prognostication time (the point from which the outcome was predicted) was frequently omitted. The included studies provided data for three of our outcomes of interest. We did not consider any of the studies to be at an overall low risk of bias for any of the outcomes analysed. We judged the certainty of the evidence as moderate to low due to imprecision and risk of bias. We found moderate-certainty evidence (due to imprecision) that for female patients there is likely a small but clinically important reduction in all-cause mortality at 30 days (odds ratio (OR) 0.81, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.72 to 0.92; I2 = 0%; absolute risk difference (ARD) 24 fewer deaths in women per 1000 participants, 95% CI 35 to 10 fewer; 2 studies, 17,627 participants). However, the remaining review outcomes do not indicate lower mortality in female patients. There is low-certainty evidence (due to serious risk of bias and imprecision) indicating that for females with PE, there may be a small but clinically important increase in all-cause hospital mortality (OR 1.11, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.22; I2 = 21.7%; 95% prediction interval (PI) 0.76 to 1.61; ARD 13 more deaths in women per 1000 participants, 95% CI 0 to 26 more; 3 studies, 611,210 participants). There is also low-certainty evidence (due to very serious imprecision) indicating that there may be little to no difference between males and females in PE-related mortality at 30 days (OR 1.08, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.12; I2 = 0%; ARD 4 more deaths in women per 1000 participants, 95% CI 22 fewer to 50 more; 2 studies, 3524 participants). No study data was found for the other outcomes, including sex-specific mortality data at one year. Moreover, due to insufficient studies, many of our planned methods were not implemented. In particular, we were unable to conduct assessments of heterogeneity or publication bias or subgroup and sensitivity analyses.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: The evidence is uncertain about sex (being male or female) as an independent prognostic factor for predicting mortality in adults with PE. We found that, for female patients with PE, there is likely a small but clinically important reduction in all-cause mortality at 30 days relative to male patients. However, this result should be interpreted cautiously, as the remaining review outcomes do not point to an association between being female and having a lower risk of death. In fact, the evidence in the review also suggested that, in female patients, there may be a small but clinically important increase in all-cause hospital mortality. It also showed that there may be little to no difference in PE-related mortality at 30 days between male and female patients. There is currently no study evidence from longitudinal studies for our other review outcomes. Although the available evidence is conflicting and therefore cannot support a recommendation for or against routinely considering sex to quantify prognosis or to guide personalised therapeutic approaches for patients with PE, this Cochrane review offers information to guide future primary research and systematic reviews.

documents.title: Safety and efficacy of bariatric or metabolic surgery in septuagenarians: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Increasing life expectancy has expanded the older population of adults living with obesity. Effective and sustainable treatment strategies are essential, due to the significant impact of obesity in the elderly on health care systems. We aimed to determine the safety of metabolic/bariatric surgery in septuagenarians.
METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published up to 31 December 2024, using Boolean logic and MeSH terms. Eligible studies involved patients aged ≥70 years undergoing primary bariatric or metabolic surgery that reported on 30-day morbidity and mortality, length of hospital stay, weight loss outcomes (BMI, %TWL, %EWL), and improvements in comorbidities. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment using the ROBINS-I tool, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer. Publication bias was assessed via funnel plots and Egger's test. Data were pooled using a random-effects model.
RESULTS: Out of 5000 articles, 12 studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising 197,194 patients, including 2528 septuagenarians. Septuagenarians had a mean age of 73.9 ± 2.6 years, and a lower preoperative BMI (42.4 ± 8.0 kg/m 2 ) compared to younger patients (46.0 ± 7.8 kg/m 2 , P < 0.0001). In patients ≥70 years, the pooled 30-day morbidity was 9.0% (95% CI: 6.0-13.0%) and mortality 0.7% (95% CI: 0.0-1.2%). Compared to younger patients, those aged ≥70 years had higher odds of 30-day complications (OR 1.55, 95% CI: 1.26-1.91, P < 0.0001) and mortality (OR 4.31, 95% CI: 1.53-12.11, P = 0.006). No significant differences were found in hospital stay or late complications. Although postoperative BMI was similar, septuagenarians had lower %TWL and %EWL, with comparable improvements in type 2 diabetes and hypertension.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings support the feasibility of metabolic and bariatric surgery in septuagenarians, albeit with a higher short-term risk profile, necessitating careful patient selection and management.

In 2022, 890 million citizens worldwide were living with obesity[ 1 ] and this is predicted to rise to 1.53 billion individuals by 2035[ 2 ]. Concurrently, the global population is aging. Throughout the 20th century, life expectancy at birth in high-income countries increased by around 30 years, primarily due to significant progress in public health measures and medical advancements[ 3 ], leading to a proportional increase in older people living with obesity. As both aging and obesity impose significant burdens on health care systems, identifying effective and sustainable treatments for this population is increasingly essential. HIGHLIGHTS The proportion of older adults living with obesity is increasing but very little is known about the safety and efficacy of bariatric surgery in this population. In this systematic review and meta-analysis that included 2528 patients aged ≥70 years (out of a total of 197 194 patients), older patients had significantly higher rates of short-term complications than younger patients but there were no significant differences in post-surgery body mass index and improvement in type 2 diabetes between the groups. Bariatric surgery is an effective weight management option that should be offered to carefully selected septuagenarians with obesity. Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) has emerged as the most effective long-term intervention for obesity, offering sustained weight loss, resolution of comorbidities, improved quality of life, and extended life expectancy [ 4 , 5 ] . While there has been a considerable increase in MBS procedures performed in patients aged 60 years and above over the past decade [ 6 , 7 ] , patients older than 70 years old are often considered at higher risk compared to younger individuals. Aging naturally leads to a reduction in physiological reserve and functional ability, making older adults more susceptible to frailty. Similarly, frailty is linked to unfavorable outcomes, prolonged hospital stays, loss of independence, and an elevated risk of complications and mortality following surgery[ 8 ]. However, while frailty often correlates with older age, chronological age alone is not a reliable predictor of surgical outcomes [ 9 , 10 ] . Considering these factors, MBS in septuagenarians remains a topic of debate. The aim of the present study is to synthesize current evidence in this important patient group, providing a more reliable analysis of the impact of MBS on perioperative morbidity, weight loss and metabolic outcomes compared to younger individuals. Material and methods Search strategy, study selection, and data extraction A systematic review was conducted following Cochrane recommendations[ 11 ] and according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)[ 12 ] guidelines and reported in line with Assessing the Methodological Quality of Systematic Review (AMSTAR) Guidelines[ 13 ]. A comprehensive search strategy was conducted with the assistance of a professional research librarian using Pubmed/MEDLINE, Embase (both via Ovid), Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, Scopus and Web of Science databases, using Boolean logic and Medical Subject Heading (MeSH) terms. We searched for publications between database inception and 31 December 2024. Eligible studies were required to contain terms related to “bariatric surgery,” “metabolic surgery,” “septuagenarians,” “elderly.” The detailed search strategy is provided in the Supplementary material (Supplementary Digital Content material 1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). To ensure a comprehensive search, the reference lists of articles and reviews were manually screened. All eligible studies published in peer-reviewed journals were included in the study analysis. Covidence software ( www.covidence.org ) was used to manage uploaded studies. Two authors independently conducted the article selection process, initially screening titles and abstracts followed by a full-text assessment for eligibility and inclusion. Any articles that did not meet the inclusion criteria were appropriately identified and excluded. In cases where discrepancies arose during the selection process, a third author was consulted, and consensus was reached. Relevant information, including study characteristics and patient demographics were extracted from each included article by two authors independently using a customized form specifically created for this study. Eligibility criteria, objectives, and outcomes Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective controlled studies, matched cohort studies, retrospective cohort and case-control studies were considered for inclusion; whereas reviews, editorials, case reports, conference abstracts, and meta-analyses were excluded. The inclusion criteria encompassed patients aged ≥70 years undergoing primary MBS [Roux en Y gastric bypass (RYGB), sleeve gastrectomy (SG), laparoscopic adjustable gastric band (LAGB), one anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB), single anastomosis with duodenal switch (SADS), equivalent to single anastomosis duodeno-ileal bypass with sleeve gastrectomy (SADI-S)]. The exclusion criteria included (1) studies that presented data only for patients aged <70 years; (2) revisional MBS. The primary objective was to assess postoperative outcomes, including overall morbidity and mortality within 30 days of surgery, as well as length of stay (LoS) if available. Additionally, weight loss outcomes, such as postoperative body mass index (BMI), percentage of total weight loss (%TWL), and percentage of excess weight loss (%EWL), were evaluated. The secondary objective focused on the improvement or resolution of obesity-related comorbidities, specifically hypertension (HTN) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). For clarity, the terms septuagenarians and patients aged ≥70 years are used interchangeably throughout this manuscript to refer to the study population. This review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO, the international register of systematic reviews. Risk of bias assessment The risk of bias (RoB) for the included studies was assessed using the Risk of Bias In Non-randomised Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I). Each study received a low, moderate, serious, or critical risk of bias in seven domains: confounding; selection of participants; classification of interventions; deviation from intended interventions; missing data; measurement of outcomes, and selection of reported results. Each study was independently reviewed by two authors, and discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion to ensure consensus. The ROBINS-I ratings were presented using the robvis tool as “traffic light” plots[ 14 ]. Funnel plots were visually inspected for asymmetry, and Egger’s test was applied to quantify bias in outcomes from more than 10 studies, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05. Statistical analysis All analyses were performed using STATA version 18.5 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). P values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and I 2 statistic, which quantifies the proportion of total variability across studies due to heterogeneity. I 2 values of 25%, 50%, and 75% were considered to indicate low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively[ 15 ]. Regardless of heterogeneity, the random effects restricted maximum likelihood model was used to pool results, as it provides more robust-effect estimates than fixed-effect models. Forest plots were generated to visualize the results, presenting individual study estimates, and the overall pooled effects. Outcomes reported on different scales were standardized to ensure comparability across studies. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed, systematically removing individual studies to assess their influence on the pooled effect estimates. To address between-study heterogeneity, subgroup analyses were performed when feasible, based on available study-level characteristics such as type of MBS. Proportion meta-analysis A single-arm meta-analysis was performed to aggregate data from all eligible studies reporting outcomes of interest in septuagenarians undergoing MBS. Proportion rates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used for binary endpoints while pooled means with 95% CIs were calculated for continuous outcomes. Comparative meta-analysis A subgroup of studies with a comparator cohort (patients younger than 70 years) was included in a comparative meta-analysis. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs were used for dichotomous variables and mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were calculated for continuous variables. Artificial intelligence (AI) was not used in the research or manuscript development and this work has been reported in line with TITAN criteria[ 16 ]. The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report. Results Study selection The initial search yielded 5000 potentially relevant articles (Fig. 1 ). After removal of duplicates and abstract screening, 39 articles were selected for full-text review. Studies that did not meet the predefined inclusion criteria were excluded from further analysis. Articles that did not meet the selection criteria and reasons for their rejection are detailed in the Supplementary material (Supplementary Digital Content material 2, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 , excluded articles). Ultimately, 12 studies [ 17 – 28 ] satisfied the inclusion criteria and were included in the final analysis (Table 1 ). Figure 1. PRISMA Flowchart. The weighted preoperative mean BMI was 42.4 ± 8.0 kg/m 2 for the older group while in the <70 years group it was 46.0 ± 7.8 kg/m 2 ( P < 0.0001). For patients aged <70 years, late complications were more frequently reported and included epigastric pain, reflux, strictures, chronic diarrhoea, and multiple reoperations. The meta-analysis of all studies reported an overall 30-day morbidity rate of 9.2% (95% CI: 5.8%–12.6%), with individual study proportions ranging from 0.9%[ 23 ] to 26.0%[ 26 ]. Heterogeneity was substantial (I 2 = 80.56%), indicating high variability among studies (Supplementary Digital Content material Sp1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). The Egger’s P -value was 0.044, suggesting a statistically significant small-study effect. This indicates a potential risk of publication bias, meaning smaller studies might be reporting more extreme effects. The funnel plot (Supplementary Digital Content material Sp1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ) also visually suggests asymmetry, further supporting this interpretation. A subgroup analysis of seven studies [ 19 , 21 , 24 – 28 ] reporting 30-day morbidity specifically for RYGB showed a pooled complication rate of 10.8% (95% CI: 7.7%–13.9%). Heterogeneity was low (I 2 = 25.5%), suggesting consistency across studies (Supplementary Digital Content material Sp1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). A subgroup meta-analysis of seven studies [ 17 , 19 , 20 , 24 , 26 , 27 ] reporting 30-day morbidity following SG showed a pooled complication rate of 6.6% (95% CI: 5.2%–7.9%). Heterogeneity was negligible (I 2 = 0.07%), indicating high consistency across studies. Given the disproportionate influence of one study (Pechman et al[ 25 ].), which contributed nearly 59% of the total weight, a sensitivity analysis was performed excluding it. The resulting pooled morbidity rate was 6.7% (95% CI: 3.2%–10.1%), with low heterogeneity (I 2 = 26.1%) (Supplementary Digital Content material Sp1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). Patients aged ≥70 years had a 0.7% risk of 30-day mortality (95% CI: 0.0%–1.2%), as estimated from the 12 studies. Mortality proportions ranged from 0.0% to 1.0%, with the highest number of deaths reported in Pechman et al[ 25 ] (1%, 95% CI: 0.5%–1.5%). The overall mortality estimate was statistically significant (Z = 2.97, P = 0.0030). Furthermore, heterogeneity was low (I 2 = 15.99%), indicating minimal variability across studies (Supplementary Digital Content material Sp2, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). The Egger’s P -value was 0.23, indicating that there was no small-study effect. The funnel plot appears symmetrical, suggesting the absence of publication bias. Patients aged ≥70 years had a 3.5% risk of 30-day readmission (95% CI: 1.5%–5.5%), based on eight studies [ 17 , 20 – 24 , 27 , 28 ] . Individual study proportions varied, with the highest readmission rate reported by Al-Kurd et al [ 17 ] at 10% (95% CI: 0.0%–20.7%), while several studies reported 0% readmission. Heterogeneity was moderate (I 2 = 33.11%), suggesting some variability among studies but no major inconsistencies (Supplementary Digital Content material Sp3, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). Patients aged ≥70 years had a significantly higher risk of experiencing 30-day complications compared to those <70 years, as reported by six studies [ 17 , 18 , 20 , 24 , 25 , 27 ] . The pooled OR was 1.55 (95% CI: 1.26–1.91; P < 0.0001), indicating 55% increased odds of complications in the older cohort. However, heterogeneity was low (I 2 = 15.21%), suggesting consistency in reported outcomes across studies (Supplementary Digital Content material S1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). Patients aged ≥70 years had a significantly higher risk of 30-day mortality compared to their younger counterparts [ 17 , 18 , 20 , 24 , 25 , 27 ] . The meta-analysis yielded an OR of 4.31 (95% CI: 1.53–12.11; P = 0.006), indicating a more than fourfold increased risk. Heterogeneity was moderate (I 2 = 35.40%), reflecting some variability among studies (Supplementary Digital Content material S2, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). A sensitivity analysis excluding the study by Pechman et al [ 25 ], which accounted for almost half of the total weight in the primary analysis, was performed to assess the robustness of the findings. The updated pooled OR decreased to 2.17 (95% CI: 0.70–6.70); however, the association was no longer statistically significant ( P = 0.178). Heterogeneity was absent (I 2 = 0%), suggesting consistency among the remaining studies. Based on data from three studies [ 17 , 20 , 27 ] with no heterogeneity (I 2 = 0%), there was no statistically significant difference in the risk of readmission within 30 days in patients aged ≥70 years compared with younger patients (OR 1.33 [0.93-1.89], P = 0.1193) (Supplementary Digital Content material S3, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). The meta-analysis of four studies [ 17 , 18 , 20 , 25 ] , including 1582 patients aged ≥70 years and 162 979 patients <70 years, found no statistically significant difference in LoS. The MD was 0.37 days (95% CI: − 0.01 to 0.76; P = 0.0579), with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 80.90%) (Supplementary Digital Content material S4, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). To explore potential differences by procedure, a subgroup analysis was conducted for studies reporting LoS following SG only. Based on two studies [ 17 , 20 ] , the pooled mean difference in LoS between patients aged ≥70 years and <70 years was 0.04 days (95% CI:−0.23 to 0.30), with no observed heterogeneity (I 2 = 0%), indicating no significant difference between age groups. In contrast, a separate subgroup analysis of studies reporting LoS following SG and RYGB combined [ 18 , 25 ] showed a significantly longer hospital stay in patients ≥70 years, with a pooled mean difference of 0.70 days (95% CI: 0.58 to 0.82) and no heterogeneity (I 2 = 0%) (Supplementary Digital Content material S4, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). Only three studies reported late complications both in patients aged ≥70 years and patients aged <70 years [ 18 , 20 , 24 ] . No significant differences were found between groups, OR 0.82 (95% CI: 0.22-3.02; P = 0.76) with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 66.3%) (Supplementary Digital Content material S5, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). As part of the single-arm meta-analysis, pooled estimates were calculated for other outcomes in patients aged ≥70 years (Supplementary Digital Content material Sp4-10, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). To explore potential sources of heterogeneity, subgroup analyses were performed based on procedure type (SG and RYGB) where data were available. A summary of key outcomes (%TWL, % EWL, and resolution or improvement of T2DM and HTN) is presented in Table 4 . While RYGB was generally associated with higher point estimates compared to SG, heterogeneity remained substantial across most outcomes, limiting the strength of comparative conclusions. Table 4 Summary of pooled outcomes in patients aged ≥70 years undergoing metabolic bariatric surgery (MBS) Outcome Number of Studies All Procedures (95% CI) SG (95% CI) RYGB (95% CI) I 2 (%) (All/SG/RYGB) All/SG/RYGB %TWL 7/4/3 25.7% (22.1–29.3) 23.8% (19.7–27.9) 30.8% (27.9–32.3) 96.8/95.4/78.4 %EWL 9/5/5 56.7% (49.8–63.5) 51.8% (40.2–63.4) 66.3% (57.4–75.2) 96.0/96.4/95.9 T2DM 11/5/5 0.69 (0.56–0.82) 0.58 (0.28–0.87) 0.74 (0.52–0.95) 87.6/96.2/92.1 HTN 11/5/5 0.44 (0.30–0.58) 0.44 (0.18–0.69) 0.37 (0.20–0.54) 93.8/97.3/86.1 Outcomes presented include percentage of total weight loss (%TWL), percentage of excess weight loss (%EWL), and estimates of proportions of patients achieving remission or improvement in type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and hypertension (HTN) following all MBS procedures, sleeve gastrectomy (SG) alone and Roux en Y gastric bypass (RYGB) alone (Supplementary material Sp7, Sp8, Sp9, Sp10). Postoperative BMI [ 17 , 18 , 20 ] showed no significant difference between groups (MD = 0.16; 95% CI: − 2.99 to 3.30; P = 0.92; I 2 = 73.23%). Given the high heterogeneity of the postoperative BMI analysis, a subgroup meta-analysis of two studies reporting BMI following SG only showed a pooled mean difference of 1.68 kg/m 2 (95% CI: 0.01 to 3.36), indicating post-operative BMI is higher in patients aged ≥70 years. Heterogeneity was absent (I 2 = 0%), indicating consistency between studies. While the result approached statistical significance ( P = 0.049), it should be interpreted with caution given the small number of included studies. However, %TWL and %EWL [ 17 , 20 , 24 , 27 ] were significantly lower in patients aged ≥70 years compared to younger patients. The MD for %TWL was −2.69 (95% CI: − 2.91 to −2 .46; P < 0.0001), and for %EWL, it was −2.72 (95% CI: − 3.12 to −2.31; P < 0 .0001), both showing no heterogeneity (I 2 = 0%) (Supplementary Digital Content material S6-S8, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). No significant differences were observed in T2DM remission/improvement (OR = 0.99; 95% CI: 0.702–1.418; P = 0.99) or HTN remission/improvement (OR = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.315–1.209; P = 0.16), with low and moderate heterogeneity (I 2 = 5.09% and 41.74%, respectively) [ 17 , 18 , 20 , 24 , 27 ] (Supplementary Digital Content material S9-S10, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/F71 ). A summary of the individual assessment of each study included in the meta-analysis is shown in SF1. A total of 11 studies were classified as having a moderate risk of bias, whereas one study[ 27 ] was classified as having a serious risk of bias. The main concerns in the studies classified as having a moderate risk of bias included confounding and selection of participants due to their retrospective nature. In the study classified as having a serious risk of bias, the main source of bias was potential missing data. Discussion This meta-analysis provides the most comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding the safety and outcomes of MBS in patients aged ≥70 years. Our findings indicate that MBS in septuagenarians is associated with a significantly higher risk of perioperative morbidity and mortality compared to younger individuals. While there is evidence of meaningful weight loss and improvement in obesity-related comorbidities, these benefits must be carefully weighed against the elevated surgical risks in this age group. Even though the single-arm 30-day mortality was 0.7% (95% CI: 0.0%—1.2%), the comparative analysis revealed that septuagenarians had a more than fourfold increased risk of perioperative mortality compared to younger individuals (OR = 4.31; 95% CI: 1.53–12.11; P = 0.006). However, the sensitivity analysis excluding Pechman et al [ 25 ], which contributed over 47% of the weight in the primary meta-analysis, revealed that this association was no longer statistically significant (OR 2.17; 95% CI: 0.70-6.70; P = 0.178). Procedure-specific subgroup analyses within the single-arm analysis offer important context for interpreting 30-day morbidity in septuagenarians undergoing MBS. The observed difference between RYGB and SG (10.8% vs. 6.6%, respectively) suggests that SG may be associated with a more favorable short-term safety profile in this age group. Importantly, the low heterogeneity observed in both subgroup analyses enhances confidence in the consistency of these estimates across studies. These findings are consistent with prior research indicating that, in this age group, SG tends to carry a lower risk of early postoperative complications than RYGB [ 29 , 30 ] . n contrast, long-term complication analysis did not demonstrate differences between the younger and older groups. Although revisional surgery was reported in some studies, its frequency did not significantly differ between age groups, suggesting that older patients tolerate primary MBS relatively well when appropriately selected. These findings align with previous studies [ 19 , 31 ] suggesting that age alone should not be an exclusion criterion for MBS but must be considered and on a case-by-case basis, with thorough preoperative evaluation and optimization. With the growing use of minimally invasive surgical techniques and the implementation of enhanced recovery after surgery protocols, postoperative outcomes following MBS have significantly improved, leading to a steady reduction in hospital stay. [ 32 – 34 ] Nevertheless, septuagenarians are a population who need special attention. Indications for MBS in patients in their seventies are generally consistent with those for younger adults, with careful consideration of physiologic age, frailty, and functional status. The American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS) and the International Federation for the Surgery of Obesity (IFSO) endorse MBS in patients aged 70 years and older, stating that chronological age alone should not be a contraindication if the patient is otherwise an appropriate surgical candidate[ 35 ]. Potential advantages for septuagenarians include marked and sustained improvements in metabolic diseases, reduction in medication burden, and improved quality of life. In fact, studies consistently show that while the absolute magnitude of weight loss and comorbidity resolution may be somewhat lower than in younger cohorts, the clinical benefits remain substantial and durable in this age group [ 36 , 37 ] . Frailty is a key determinant of surgical risk in older adults and is increasingly recognized as a more relevant predictor of postoperative outcomes than chronological age alone. It encompasses a range of physiological impairments, including decreased muscle strength, reduced functional reserve, and an increased inflammatory state, all of which can predispose patients to poorer surgical outcomes [ 38 , 39 ] . Preoperative frailty assessment tools, such as the Clinical Frailty Scale and Edmonton Frail Scale[ 40 ], have been proposed as essential components in the preoperative evaluation of elderly patients undergoing surgery. Studies have shown that frail individuals have a significantly higher risk of postoperative complications, longer hospital stays, and increased mortality[ 41 ]. The American Society of Anaesthesiologists, the American College of Surgeons and the American Geriatrics Society recommend a comprehensive preoperative assessment among older adults that includes not only evaluation of frailty but also cognitive function, functional status, nutritional status, polypharmacy, and psychosocial factors [ 42 , 43 ] . Unfortunately, none of the studies in this meta-analysis reported formal frailty metrics or preoperative optimization, and only two (Belluzzi et al [ 19 ] and Pechman et al [ 25 ]) described functional status in broad terms such as independence or dependence. The absence of standardized frailty data limits the ability to stratify risk more precisely in our analysis. Nevertheless, we strongly believe that incorporating a thorough preoperative geriatric assessment into clinical decision-making alongside the bariatric multidisciplinary team (MDT) may improve patient selection and optimize perioperative care strategies to mitigate surgical risks in this population. Our study demonstrates significant weight loss following MBS. However, the extent of weight reduction was slightly lower compared to younger individuals. Several mechanisms may explain the attenuated weight loss response among this patient group. Elderly and frail patients often exhibit dysregulation of key metabolic pathways, including chronic inflammation and altered gut hormone responses [ 44 , 45 ] , all of which are potential causes of attenuated postoperative weight loss. Furthermore, reduced physical activity and sarcopenia, both common among older cohorts, can lead to lower energy expenditure and reduced capacity for postoperative lifestyle modifications, negatively contributing to this issue [ 46 – 48 ] . With regards to comorbidity improvement or resolution, MBS in patients ≥70 years old did not show differences in comparison to younger individuals in our meta-analysis. MBS improves insulin sensitivity, pancreatic β-cell function and induces gut hormone changes in people living with T2DM [ 49 – 51 ] . However, it has been demonstrated that patients with longstanding T2DM may experience lower remissions rates and later disease relapse [ 52 , 53 ] . Since advanced T2DM at the time of surgery is one of the strongest predictors of diabetes relapse, it is likely that patients ≥70 years old undergoing MBS had a longer disease duration, making them less likely to achieve remission. However, due to limitations within the included studies, we were unable to stratify patients based on diabetes duration, as this information was not consistently reported. Similarly, reductions in antihypertensive medication use were observed. This fact supports the cardiovascular benefits of MBS among this patient group despite the expected vascular aging and reduced autonomic adaptability [ 53 , 54 ] , which might impact improvement of hypertension. This study has several limitations, the most important being the quality and design of the included studies. All were retrospective observational studies, which are inherently prone to selection bias, confounding, and other limitations in internal validity. Using the ROBINS-I tool, 11 studies were assessed as having a moderate risk of bias and one as having serious risk of bias. Accordingly, the meta-analysis is based on evidence of generally low methodological quality. This restricts the strength and certainty of the conclusions, and the results should therefore be interpreted with appropriate caution. While the findings suggest that MBS may be feasible and effective in selected septuagenarian patients, more robust prospective data are needed to support these outcomes. Another key limitation of our analysis is the high heterogeneity observed in long-term complications (I 2 = 66.3%) and BMI changes (I 2 = 73.23%), probably due to differences in study design, operative technique, comorbidity burden and/or duration, and definitions of adverse events. Furthermore, while perioperative outcomes, weight loss, and comorbidity resolution were assessed, functional outcomes and quality-of-life improvements were not reported. While our findings suggest that MBS may offer meaningful benefits in terms of weight loss and comorbidity improvement for selected patients aged ≥70 years, these results must be interpreted with caution. Therefore, MBS in septuagenarians should be considered on an individual basis, following a thorough MDT assessment. Given the rising prevalence of obesity in older populations, future high-quality prospective studies are needed to evaluate safety, functional outcomes, and quality of life to better guide decision-making in this specific demographic. Conclusion This meta-analysis suggests that MBS may be a feasible and beneficial option for well-selected patients aged ≥70 years, offering significant weight loss and metabolic benefits despite higher perioperative risks relative to younger patients. Age alone should not be a contraindication, but decisions should be individualized. Future high-quality prospective studies are needed to better define optimal patient selection criteria and assess outcomes in this growing population. documents.title: Efficacy of tranexamic acid in reducing perioperative blood transfusions and thrombosis in liver surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Preventing bleeding during the perioperative period is critically important in liver surgery and mismanagement can raise the need for transfusions as well as the rates of morbidity and death. Tranexamic acid (TXA) has been shown to effectively decrease perioperative bleeding in patients with trauma, some studies have also shown that TXA plays the same role in liver surgery. The effectiveness of TXA in hepatectomy and liver transplantation was reassessed in this meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, which included recently published studies.
METHODS: The PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase databases were comprehensively searched to identify studies that were published from January 1947 to September 2024. Results related to transfusion requirements, incidents of thromboembolism, and the number of deaths were retrieved from the included studies. The data were quantified using random effects models.
RESULTS: A total of 1674 patients were included in the seven studies. The results showed no discernible difference between the TXA and control groups regarding the reduction in perioperative transfusion needs (OR 0.24; 95% CI 0.03 ~ 1.87) and the final mortality rate (OR 0.99; 95% CI 0.48 ~ 2.06) during hepatectomy and transplantation, however, TXA increased the incidence of thromboembolism (OR 1.74; 95% CI 1.01 ~ 3.01).
CONCLUSIONS: TXA does not reduce perioperative transfusion requirements during liver resection and transplantation and has no significant effect on the final mortality rate; however, TXA does increase the incidence of thromboembolic events.

Introduction Due to the estimated incidence of liver cancer, which will be more than 1 million cases by 2025, it still has to deal with the disease worldwide [ 1 ]. Individuals diagnosed with liver cancer can choose from several treatment approaches [ 2 ]. Liver surgery remains one of the most challenging abdominal procedures to date because of its intricate anatomy and abundant blood supply, which makes up about 20% of the cardiac output in a single cycle, making it one of the most technically difficult procedures [ 3 ]. Despite advances in surgical and nonsurgical treatment techniques for liver surgery, bleeding remains a major perioperative risk. Liver transplantation and resection are primarily performed in patients who have significant changes in coagulation factors, flora, and organ function; and patient who are at significant risk of blood loss during liver surgery. Over the course of surgery, 22–27% of patients who have liver resection get al.logeneic red blood cells transfusions [ 4 ]. Blood transfusions are associated with considerable risks, such as acute lung injury related to transfusion, severe allergic responses, infections, immune incompatibility, and even fatal outcomes [ 5 ]. Since it was first used in 1966 [ 6 ], tranexamic acid (TXA) has been applied to treat a wide range of conditions effectively and routinely, including skin diseases [ 7 ] and craniocerebral injury [ 8 ]. The mechanism underlying the effect of TXA is thought to involve the inhibition of tissue fibrinolysis, thereby stabilizing blood clots [ 9 ]. TXA has been used for decades as an antifibrinolytic agent to treat trauma, surgery, postpartum hemorrhage, and other indications [ 10 ]. TXA binds to fibrinogen and fibrinolytic enzymes, producing an antifibrinolytic effect that helps minimize blood loss; it also has a protective effect on endothelial cells and beneficially modulates inflammatory and other responses after ischemia and reperfusion [ 11 ]. The NICE transfusion guidelines that were published in 2016 stated that adults who were to undergo surgery and were expected to have moderate blood loss should also receive TXA [ 12 ], but few NICE-related trials involving liver surgery have been performed, making it difficult to extrapolate this result to the field of liver surgery. Contemporary transfusion practices follow WHO blood safety standards, but operational thresholds vary nationally: AABB (US/Canada) recommends transfusion for Hb < 7 g/dL in stable patients [ 13 ], while ESA (Europe) suggests < 8 g/dL [ 14 ], and JST (Japan) permits > 8 g/dL in hepatic surgery [ 15 ]. This institutional heterogeneity may influence TXA efficacy assessments. A meta-analysis published in 2021 [ 16 ] suggested that TXA can safely reduce the need to transfuse blood when resecting and transplanting the liver. On the basis of this literature, this article summarizes additional literature and randomized controlled trial samples and reconducts a systematic review and meta-analysis. Methods Although the systematic review had predefined methods of analysis, documented and clearly outlined, the protocol was not officially recorded. A comprehensive search of the Embase, PubMed and Web of Science databases was performed to determine relevant studies published before December 2024. The search combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and keywords related to TXA with those related to hepatic surgery, as described below: [“Tranexamic Acid ” OR “AMCHA” OR “trans-4-(Aminomethyl)cyclohexanecarboxylic Acid” OR “Cyklokapron” OR “Ugurol” OR “Transamin” OR “KABI2161” OR “Amchafibrin” OR “Anvitoff” OR “Spotof” OR “Exacyl”] AND [(“liver” OR “hepatic”) AND (“surgery” OR “transplant”)] [ 17 ]. This systematic review and meta-analysis followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [ 18 ], as presented in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 PRISMA 2020 flow diagram The eligible types of studies were randomized controlled trials that evaluated intravenous TXA in the perioperative period after liver resection and transplantation versus a control group (placebo or no treatment). Participants were required to be ≥ 18 years old. We excluded: systematic reviews, retrospective studies; studies evaluating non-TXA antifibrinolytics; studies where TXA was not the sole intervention or lacked a control group; studies comparing TXA to an active comparator; and studies of non-hepatic surgery. Two reviewers independently evaluated the search results to identify potentially relevant studies, whose full texts were then obtained and reviewed to determine eligibility for inclusion and exclusion. Data abstraction and risk of bias assessment A standardized data form was prepared to record the study characteristics and results, which included information on the study type, surgery type, target population, and treatment outcomes. The number of perioperative transfusions patients, incidents of thromboembolism and deaths were the outcomes of interest. Each study was assigned a modified overall risk of bias score: low, moderate, or high risk of bias. The following domains were assessed for each study: bias introduced during randomization, bias due to deviation away from the planned intervention, bias arising from missing result data, inaccurate measurement of outcomes, and selective reporting bias [ 19 ]. A risk of bias table was constructed via the ROB2 assessment tool. There was no disagreement among the reviewers on the risk of bias assessment. Data analysis Meta-analysis of the combined data was performed using Stata software (StataMP v18.0 http://www.stata.com ). Odds ratios (OR) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI) are used to summarise effects for dichotomous outcomes. The I 2 statistic was employed to evaluate the statistical heterogeneity among the studies included, with thresholds of 25%, 50%, and 75% representing low, moderate, and high levels of heterogeneity, respectively [ 20 ]. A fixed-effects model was applied when P exceeded 0.1 and I 2 was below 50%, whereas a random-effects model was employed when P was less than 0.1 and I 2 exceeded 50%. Funnel plot asymmetry tests should only be applied when the meta-analysis encompasses a minimum of 10 studies [ 21 ]. The asymmetry of the funnel plots was visually inspected according to the primary outcome. Subgroup analyses were performed post hoc to explore sources of heterogeneity, specifically for surgery type (resection/transplantation). These were not pre-specified in the original protocol. Results Research characteristics The studies incorporated in the analysis spanned publications from 1993 to 2024 (Table 1 ). There are three North American, two Asian and two European studies. Five studies included the liver transplant population [ 22 – 26 ], and two studies included the liver resection population [ 27 , 28 ]. All included trials (7/7) administered TXA intravenously. No studies used oral TXA, eliminating route-related heterogeneity. The results showed no discernible difference between the TXA and control groups, and TXA failed to reduce total percentage of patients needing perioperative transfusion (OR 0.24; 95% CI 0.03 ~ 1.87). Three studies [ 22 , 23 , 26 ] reported no thromboembolic incidents in either group. In the three other trials documenting thromboembolic events, a notable difference was observed between the TXA group and the control group, indicating that TXA raised the risk of thromboembolism in patients (OR 1.74; 95% CI 1.01 ~ 3.01) (Fig. 3 ). The follow-up periods in these studies varied from one month to twelve months. In one study, the follow-up period was not clearly defined. In the four trials with deaths, the results showed no discernible difference between the TXA and control groups (OR 0.99; 95% CI 0.48 ~ 2.06) (Fig. 4 ). A total of 3 studies on perioperative blood transfusion needs were included, including 2 studies in the liver resection subgroup and 1 study in the liver transplantation subgroup. The results are shown in Fig. 5 . In the liver resection subgroup, the results showed no discernible difference between the TXA and control groups, and TXA failed to reduce the overall proportion of patients who received perioperative blood transfusions after liver resection (OR 0.21; 95% CI 0.00 ~ 11.78). No subgroup analysis was performed with the liver transplantation subgroup since only one article evaluated patients in this subgroup. Fig. 5 Subgroup analysis results in perioperative blood transfusion needs A total of 3 studies on thromboembolic events were included, including 1 study in the liver resection subgroup and 2 studies in the liver transplantation subgroup. The results are shown in Fig. 6 . In the liver transplantation subgroup, the results showed no discernible difference between the TXA and control groups, and TXA failed to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events after liver transplantation (OR 2.22; 95% CI 0.47 ~ 10.43). No subgroup analysis was performed for the liver resection subgroup because it contained only 1 study. Fig. 6 Subgroup analysis results in thromboembolic events A total of 4 studies on the impact of mortality were included, including 1 study in the liver resection subgroup and 3 studies in the liver transplantation subgroup. The results are shown in Fig. 7 . In the liver transplantation subgroup, the results showed no discernible difference between the TXA and control groups., and TXA failed to affect the mortality rate of patients after liver transplantation (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.13 ~ 2.76); no subgroup analysis was performed in the liver resection subgroup because there was only 1 study. The three subgroup analyses described above were performed via random effects models. Fig. 7 Subgroup analysis results in impact on mortality Risk of bias Among the seven RCTs that were included in this review, most (57%) had a moderate risk of bias, two (29%) had a low risk of bias, and one (14%) had a high risk of bias (Fig. 8 ). Bias risk was assessed using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB.2), with assessment criteria following its guidelines [ 29 ], as detailed in the supplementary content. Fig. 8 Risk of bias assessment for RCTs Protocol registration The protocol for this systematic review is registered on PROSPERO (Registration CRD42025649262). Discussion The use of TXA in bleeding trauma patients has been widely accepted since the CRASH-2 trial, which evaluated the benefits of TXA in trauma patients [ 30 ]. A systematic review published in 2013 [ 31 ] concluded that TXA decreases blood loss in surgical patients by roughly one-third. This phenomenon has also been widely demonstrated in trauma [ 32 ] and orthopedic surgery [ 33 ] patients, and a systematic review published in 2023 [ 34 ] suggested that TXA is a safe treatment that reduces perioperative blood loss but does not affect wound healing or infection rates. A 2021 systematic review [ 35 ], which analyzed 71 trials involving 7539 patients, found that topical TXA application decreased the need for blood transfusions during adult surgeries without being linked to any adverse effects. Nevertheless, none of these trials assessed TXA use during liver surgery, and it cannot be inferred that the use of TXA during liver resection or liver transplantation would yield exactly the same results. In recent years, several scholars have proposed different views. A retrospective study of 779 patients undergoing liver transplantation in Germany was published in 2024 [ 36 ], and this study revealed that TXA was administered to 262 patients (33.6%)during surgery, and this treatment was not related to intraoperative blood loss or any secondary endpoints (intraoperative and postoperative red blood cell transfusion, or thrombosis). The HALT-IT trial, which was published in 2020 [ 37 ], concluded that TXA did not reduce the amount of bleeding, transfusion, or mortality associated with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding; instead, in this group of patients, TXA was associated with a significantly higher risk of venous thromboembolism. A study published in 2023 [ 38 ] revealed that the risk of pulmonary embolism was greater after the use of TXA during bone or chondrosarcoma surgery. This may be used as one of the reference opinions, but the amount of blood transfusion and transfusion requirements during orthopedic surgery are very different from those needed during liver surgery, and there are obvious differences in the basic conditions, internal environment, coagulation function and other factors between patients; thus, this topic needs further research. It is worth mentioning that the POISE-3 trial, which was published in 2025 by Park et al. [ 39 ], as a large-scale multi-centre RCT ( n = 9535), reported that TXA significantly reduced the composite bleeding risk in general surgery (HR = 0.74, 95% CI = 0.59–0.93), with a stronger protective effect observed in the hepatobiliary surgery subgroup (HR = 0.55, 95% CI = 0.34–0.91), and did not increase the risk of cardiovascular events (HR = 0.95). However, an independent analysis of liver surgery in this study found that TXA did not significantly reduce intraoperative blood loss and was associated with an increased risk of postoperative thrombotic events. We consider Park et al.‘s study to be meaningful, but since this RCT had a broad scope and did not focus specifically on liver surgery, there are differences from our study results. In the seven studies we included, the amount of blood transfused could not be determined with complete accuracy to evaluate in detail the impact of TXA on the need for blood transfusions and the amount of blood transfused. Although beyond our quantitative synthesis scope, qualitative review suggests TXA did not consistently reduce blood loss or morbidity. For instance, Karanicolas 2024 ( n = 249) observed comparable blood loss between groups (median 650mL TXA vs. 700mL placebo), while Dalmau 2000 reported lower transfusion volumes with TXA (1.8 ± 1.1 vs. 3.2 ± 2.0 units, p < 0.01). Future IPD meta-analyses may clarify these relationships. Moreover, the indications for blood transfusion are executed by doctors in different regions, and the decision about whether to administer a blood transfusion to a specific patient cannot be strictly controlled. Among included trials, transfusion triggers ranged from Hb 7 g/dL (Karanicolas 2024, Canada) to 9 g/dL (Devi 2008, India), reflecting local guideline adherence. This 2 g/dL divergence likely contributes to the observed heterogeneity in transfusion outcomes. As for why tranexamic acid may be effective in haemostasis and reducing blood transfusions in other surgical fields but ineffective in liver surgery, this may be due to the following reasons. First, almost all coagulation factors, as well as important anticoagulant proteins and fibrinolytic system regulatory proteins, are synthesised in the liver. Liver disease or extensive liver resection surgery itself can severely impair liver synthesis function, leading to a comprehensive deficiency of coagulation factors and anticoagulant/fibrinolytic regulatory proteins. TXA targets only the fibrinolytic system and cannot address this comprehensive deficiency of coagulation factors. Second, patients with advanced liver disease are not simply in a hypocoagulable state. Although coagulation factor synthesis is reduced, anticoagulant proteins are also reduced, platelet count and quality decline, and the fibrinolytic system is disrupted. This state represents a fragile rebalancing that may be more prone to developing in either the direction of bleeding or portal vein thrombosis. TXA targets only the hyperfibrinolysis component, and in this complex rebalancing system, its haemostatic effects may be masked or interfered by other defects. Forced inhibition of fibrinolysis could theoretically even increase the risk of thrombosis. This provides a plausible biological basis for the results of our meta-analysis that TXA failed to reduce transfusion requirements for liver surgery but may have increased thrombotic events. In the subgroup analysis, none of the three studies yielded statistically significant findings, and the limited number of included studies, along with the small sample size, prevented achieving satisfactory results to effectively reduce heterogeneity. Regarding the necessity of long-term follow-up, although TXA’s antifibrinolytic effect is acute, its impact on coagulation homeostasis may predispose to delayed thrombotic events in susceptible patients. For instance, portal vein thrombosis after liver transplantation typically presents at 2–4 weeks post-op. Current RCTs lack power to detect such associations due to short follow-up (median 7 days). Limitation This study has several limitations. First, the sample size of the included data varied greatly, and the dose of TXA injected and the indications for blood transfusion varied from trial to trial, resulting in great heterogeneity. In a meta-analysis published in 2017, the use of oral plus intravenous tranexamic acid was not more effective than a single injection in primary hip replacement surgery [ 40 ], indicating that the dose and efficacy of TXA may not have a simple linear relationship and that there may be confounding factors. In addition, the follow-up time after surgery was inconsistent, ranging from 1 week to 1 year, which may affect assessment of the outcome of venous thrombosis incidence and patient mortality. Third, unadjustable differences in transfusion protocols between trial sites remain a residual confounder. Forth, although our findings apply solely to IV TXA, oral administration—despite its theoretical benefits in outpatient settings—lacks evidence in liver surgery. This represents a knowledge gap for future research. Fifth, the subgroup comparisons between liver resection and transplantation were hypothesis-generating analyses conducted after observing high heterogeneity. Given the limited studies per subgroup ( n ≤ 3) and lack of pre-specification, these results require validation in dedicated RCTs. Finally, only a few eligible studies were included, partly due to the restrictive inclusion criteria. While this may affect generalizability, the consistency of effects across studies strengthens our conclusions. More convincing results may emerge as more randomized controlled trials are included. Conclusion The current analysis revealed that TXA did not reduce the need for perioperative transfusion during hepatectomy or liver transplantation, and TXA had no effect on postoperative mortality, but TXA did increase incidents of thromboembolism. However, owing to heterogeneity and sample size, a larger study with a longer follow-up time is needed to explore the direct effects of TXA on the risk of bleeding, transfusion requirements, risk of thrombosis, and mortality of patients undergoing liver surgery. Our inability to analyze transfusion volumes and composite morbidity due to data heterogeneity represents a knowledge gap meriting future study. Acknowledgements Not applicable. documents.title: Prognostic value of venous thromboembolism in patients with advanced pancreatic cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between the incidence of VTE and the prognosis of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, as there is currently a lack of systematic research on this topic, despite the prevalence of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in patients with pancreatic cancer.
METHODS: Databases including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were searched until April 9, 2023, to identify studies that explored the relationship between VTE and the prognosis of advanced pancreatic cancer. Duplicate publications, studies without full text or sufficient information for data extraction, animal experiments, reviews, and systematic reviews were excluded. The extracted data were analyzed using STATA 15.1.
RESULTS: The pooled results indicated a significant association between the incidence of VTE and poorer overall survival (HR=1.38, 95% CI: 1.24 - 1.53, p < 0.001) and disease-free survival (HR=2.42, 95% CI: 1.94 - 3.04, p < 0.001) among patients with advanced pancreatic cancer. Additionally, early VTE showed a significant impact on overall survival (HR=2.03, 95% CI: 1.33 - 3.12, p = 0.001), whereas late VTE did not demonstrate a significant association with poor overall survival (HR=1.22, 95% CI: 0.96 - 1.54, p = 0.099).
CONCLUSIONS: This study found that advanced pancreatic cancer patients with VTE had poorer overall and disease-free survival than those without. Meanwhile, the patients with early VTE had a significantly poorer prognosis, whereas late VTE did not. The findings highlight the importance of timely detection of VTE for patients with advanced pancreatic cancer patients and offer a partial theoretical basis for future clinical endeavors.

Additionally, early VTE showed a significant impact on overall survival (HR=2.03, 95% CI: 1.33 - 3.12, p = 0.001), whereas late VTE did not demonstrate a significant association with poor overall survival (HR=1.22, 95% CI: 0.96 - 1.54, p = 0.099).
